requirement:
An item with no attachments has an empty list. A language may return empty
lists for every item.
rationale:
The requirement has two parts. An item with no attachments has an empty list. A language may return empty lists for every item. The second part is a MAY, so it imposes nothing to check.

The test `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/outline_content.rs#fn[bundled_languages_classify_only_their_attachment_syntax]` carries a `{test}` reference to this requirement. It covers the first part in two ways:
- **Plain text:** For the `test.txt` case (`# just text`), it flattens the attachments of every outline item and asserts that the result equals `vec![]`. So every item in that outline has an empty list, even though the source looks like a comment.
- **Other languages:** For the other bundled languages, it asserts the exact flattened set of attachments across all items. An item that should have none, such as the `class[C]` item in the TypeScript cases or any non-annotated item elsewhere, would show up as an unexpected entry and fail the equality assertion. The `test.py` case also pins `def[f]` to exactly 3 attachments.

I read the implementation, `crates/trust-but-verify/src/outline/contents.rs#impl[OutlineItem]/fn[new]`, to see where the empty default comes from. It initialises `attachments` to `Vec::new()`. That default is a plain value with no conditional logic, so the empty-list obligation is mostly structural. The test still checks it through the plain-text case and the exact-match assertions. I found no gap.
